newsitem.title: POLAND: Chirac shows Poland it has an EU friend in France.
newsitem.headline: Chirac shows Poland it has an EU friend in France.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac on Friday left Poland reassured that, alongside Germany, it also had a firm advocate of its European Union hopes in Paris.

Chirac picked Poland for his first trip to eastern Europe and described the country of nearly 40 million people, with its fast-growing economy, as France's natural partner -- "its sister in the East."
Chirac also supported the bid by Poland -- which escaped Soviet domination in 1989 when Solidarity overthrew communism -- to bind itself to the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
But Poles were still grappling with the full implications of Chirac's emphasis on soothing and involving Russia as the NATO military alliance is expanded to include their country.
In an speech to both houses of parliament on Thursday Chirac gave Poland what its politicians crave, a clear, early target date for its entry into the European Union.
"I hope that, by the year 2000, Poland will have joined our Union," Chirac said -- echoing earlier encouragement from German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
His words during his three-day visit were contradicted by a European Commission spokesman in Brussels, who said on Friday that the earliest realistic admission date was 2002.

But they did much to undo the effect of his predecessor Francois Mitterrand's 1991 comments that it would be decades before the new, ex-communist democracies joined the EU -- entrenching a view of France as lukewarm to Polish aspirations.
President Aleksander Kwasniewski greeted them as a pledge of active support in EU entry talks, telling a news conference:
"We want to believe that France treats this date, the year 2000, as a task for Poland and a challenge for France."
"We were missing French involvement in recent years, while the Germans have been deeply engaged," said opposition party parliamentarian Piotr Nowina-Konopka.
The Gaullist Chirac's words showed a return to a vision of Europe embodied by Charles de Gaulle himself, Nowina-Konopka, a foreign affairs specialist, told Reuters.
He said the process of securing closer ties to NATO should start next year and be soon completed, though new members should join after NATO reforms.
But he said that Russia, which views NATO's inclusion of its neighbour Poland as a threat, should not be isolated.

In this context, Chirac called for a summit involving NATO's 16 existing members, candidate states from the former Soviet bloc and other countries including Russia -- which would finally lay to rest the Cold War division of Europe.

This disconcerted some Poles, hostile to any idea that Russia should have a say on their future, although French officials made clear that the conference was not intended to replace direct negotiations on NATO entry.

"It is hard to imagine that this conference should decide on the expansion of NATO. What would Russia's role be in this?" parliament's foreign affairs committee chief Bronislaw Geremek told Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper on Friday.
Nevertheless, Polish analysts saw the visit as a sign that historic ally France was rallying to join Poland's past foe Germany -- now its firmest advocate -- at their country's side.

Chirac, who wound up his trip with a visit to the southern city of Krakow and the former Auschwitz Nazi death camp on Friday, devoted much effort to promoting French trade and investment links with Poland, which have trailed Germany's.

The French president called for a strengthening of the Weimar Triangle, a loose framework for cooperation also including Germany. This prompted Kwasniewski to propose that he, Chirac and Germany's Kohl meet in Warsaw early next year.
"Chirac is saying clearly, that there are three countries who have special responsiblity for the fate of Europe," Nowina-Konopka said.
